<title>Lactose intolerance is actually the human norm – but racism, the US government and business interests have made it into a condition</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755496/original/file-20260821-50-9jl7i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The majority of the world is unable to process the lactose in milk without uncomfortable symptoms</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/lactose-intolerance-allergy-milk-bottle-splatter-royalty-free-image/2162416983">Olga Miltsova/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Lactose intolerance makes drinking milk or eating ice cream a literal pain. For some people, eating a dairy treat can lead to <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/lactose-intolerance/symptoms-causes/syc-20374232">bloating, nausea and diarrhea</a>. You might’ve experienced its effects yourself. If so, you may think of lactose intolerance as a defect rather than the norm. </p>

<p>But did you know that <a href="https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/lactose-intolerance/#frequency">most people in the world</a> today are lactose intolerant – and that the condition itself was <a href="https://doi.org/10.1515/9780824879570-014">invented in the 1960s</a>?</p>

<p>“Surely you mean discovered, not invented,” I hear you saying. I don’t. <a href="https://liberalarts.du.edu/about/people/hilary-smith">As a historian</a> who has <a href="https://press.jhu.edu/books/title/53841/nutritional-imperialism">traced the origins of nutrition-science ideas</a>, I have chosen the word “invented” on purpose.</p>

<h2>Inventing lactose intolerance</h2>

<p>Variations in people’s ability to digest lactose first came to scientists’ attention after American dairy producers found a way to rid themselves of <a href="https://idnc.library.illinois.edu/?a=d&amp;d=FWR19441011.2.2&amp;e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN----------">a postwar milk surplus</a>. To offload what they couldn’t sell, they looked to the government to intervene. And it did, <a href="https://www.fsa.usda.gov/Internet/FSA_File/mpsp04.pdf">buying the excess</a> and embedding it in school lunches and other places with publicly funded meals. </p>

<p>Suddenly, many people who had not habitually drunk milk were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1525/AA.2007.109.4.666">consuming it regularly</a>, including not only some Americans but also people overseas. Part of that same milk surplus found its way into school lunches in places such as <a href="https://recipes.hypotheses.org/17642">Japan</a> and <a href="https://www.fcdc.org.tw/en-us/summary-detail/Dependence-and-Competition:-The-Dairy-Industry-in-Taiwan-during-the-Post-War-and-US-aid-Period-(1945-1965)-i.59">Taiwan</a> in the 1950s as the American government began to sell milk to allies during the Cold War. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755790/original/file-20260824-50-hp5q4b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Black and white photo of children in uniform eating lunch at their desks" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755790/original/file-20260824-50-hp5q4b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755790/original/file-20260824-50-hp5q4b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=604&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755790/original/file-20260824-50-hp5q4b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=604&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755790/original/file-20260824-50-hp5q4b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=604&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755790/original/file-20260824-50-hp5q4b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=758&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755790/original/file-20260824-50-hp5q4b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=758&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755790/original/file-20260824-50-hp5q4b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=758&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Longshou Elementary School students in Taiwan in 1964 eat an American aid lunch for the first time.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.archives.gov.tw/tw/arctw/336-8467.html">National Archives of Taiwan</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/">CC BY-NC-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Many of the groups drinking milk regularly for the first time did not like it. In fact, it made them feel sick. Intrigued, scientists set up experiments to figure out why. In a 1966 study comparing how Black and white people incarcerated in Baltimore metabolized lactose, researchers found that Black participants had <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1966.03110120074017">lower levels of lactase</a> – the enzyme that breaks down lactose – in their guts. </p>

<p>To the white scientists conducting this study, the trouble that the Black prisoners had digesting milk looked like an “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1966.03110120074017">inborn error of metabolism</a>.” They assumed that the normal human state was lactose tolerance and that the lactose intolerant had inherited a genetic mutation.</p>

<p>It was only after years more work with research participants of many races that experts realized that, as one National Institutes of Health official put it in 1981, “lactose intolerance is a <a href="https://archive.org/details/lactosedigestion0000unse">normal physiological condition</a>, shared by every adult animal except for certain ethnic and racial groups in man.” People of northern European descent, it turned out, were the weird ones. It was their ancestors who had passed down a genetic mutation – one that made them able to digest milk after infancy.</p>

<p>In short, what scientists discovered in the 1960s was that different bodies process milk differently. What they invented was <a href="https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/lactose-intolerance/definition-facts">the idea that lactose intolerance is a defect</a>. Accepting that framing would mean nearly two-thirds of the human population – the estimated <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11894-017-0558-9">prevalence of lactose intolerance</a> worldwide – is defective. </p>

<p>Instead of acknowledging that dairy-free diets can be healthy, people innovated ways to overcome this supposed disability so everyone <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/foods12132553">could consume more</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755461/original/file-20260821-60-umrpsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Statue of cow dressed as Superman in an advertising display, two people working in the background" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755461/original/file-20260821-60-umrpsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755461/original/file-20260821-60-umrpsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755461/original/file-20260821-60-umrpsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755461/original/file-20260821-60-umrpsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755461/original/file-20260821-60-umrpsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755461/original/file-20260821-60-umrpsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755461/original/file-20260821-60-umrpsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Milk is advertised in China as essential to health, even though most of the population is lactose intolerant.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/China%20Daily%20Life/49a71fae6f2f4642b9fe318cdb592191/photo">Ng Han Guan/AP Photo</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Nutritional imperialism</h2>

<p>Lactose intolerance is one example of what I call <a href="https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/53841/nutritional-imperialism">nutritional imperialism</a>: a way of thinking that treats white diets as the norm and everyone else’s as an aberration. </p>

<p>Nutritional imperialism was <a href="http://webdoc.sub.gwdg.de/ebook/p/2005/history_cooperative/www.historycooperative.org/proceedings/interactions/laudan.html">common in the 20th century</a>, when scientists thought that not only milk-rich but also meat-heavy diets were best; they considered diets outside of the United States and Europe too vegetarian. Some also argued that wheat flour, not rice, ought to be the universal staple. </p>

<p>The same bias applied to bodies. Besides faulty lactose digestion, nonwhite bodies were accused of other failures, too, such as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1242/dmm.049601">aldehyde dehydrogenase deficiency</a>, an inability to digest alcohol quickly. The less technical term for this may be more familiar: Asian flush.</p>

<p>Such differences might have been thought of as variety, just another way of being human. Instead, each became a deficiency.</p>

<p>Many people today have inherited and perpetuated this way of thinking without knowing it, including those who are deemed deficient by it. In 1959, the director of Japan’s nutrition bureau declared that “<a href="https://www.tofugu.com/japan/history-of-ramen/">rice-eating peoples</a>” such as the Japanese were “resigned and passive” and could correct this by imitating Western diets and switching to wheat. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755462/original/file-20260821-50-l5ksk1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Grocery store aisle filled with various brands of milk" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755462/original/file-20260821-50-l5ksk1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755462/original/file-20260821-50-l5ksk1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755462/original/file-20260821-50-l5ksk1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755462/original/file-20260821-50-l5ksk1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755462/original/file-20260821-50-l5ksk1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755462/original/file-20260821-50-l5ksk1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755462/original/file-20260821-50-l5ksk1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Milk is ubiquitous in grocery stores in China.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Refrigerated_milk_at_CR_Mart_Zhaojia_Lane-20220512.jpg">Shwangtianyuan/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Today, the most prominent scientist promoting the idea that Asian flush is a disease is a <a href="https://med.stanford.edu/profiles/che-hong-chen">geneticist of Taiwanese descent</a> who started a research consortium to study “<a href="https://envmed.kmu.edu.tw/images/Stanford-Taiwan_ALDH2_Deficiency_Research_Consortium_STAR_Mission__Scope_Statement_1.pdf">the most common human enzymopathy in the world</a>.” </p>

<p>The Chinese Nutrition Society placed a tall glass of milk next to its <a href="http://dg.en.cnsoc.org/article/14/3_U0O6XTRayjKt8jhWL2kw.html">2022 Food Guide Plate</a> – never mind estimates that the vast majority of Han Chinese, the <a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/Han-Chinese">largest ethnic group in China and worldwide</a>, are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00270566">lactose intolerant</a>.</p>

<h2>Turning sickness back into difference</h2>

<p>Science that pathologizes difference <a href="https://theconversation.com/mass-deportations-dont-keep-out-bad-genes-they-use-scientific-racism-to-justify-biased-immigration-policies-243785">helps racism persist</a>. </p>

<p>In recent years, white supremacists have embraced the concept of lactose intolerance as a distinguishing debility of nonwhite people. Social media users have copied and pasted a map of the geographic distribution of lactose tolerance originally published in the scientific journal Nature into <a href="https://www.uowoajournals.org/asj/article/id/275/">racist chat threads</a> on the online discussion forum 4chan. </p>

<p>In 2017, internet trolls disrupted an anti-racist art installation with neo-Nazi chants and messily <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-the-alt-right-uses-milk-to-promote-white-supremacy-94854">downed jugs of milk</a> to accentuate their white identity.</p>

<p>Turning a lactose-digestion difference into a deficiency has done more to reinforce <a href="https://press.jhu.edu/books/title/53841/nutritional-imperialism">narratives of racial hierarchy</a> than to improve public health. So here’s a suggestion: If you enjoy eating dairy, keep doing it; if you don’t, don’t – and know that there is nothing wrong with you.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/286550/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: The majority of the world is unable to process the lactose in milk without uncomfortable symptoms Olga Miltsova/iStock via Getty Images Plus Lactose intolerance makes drinking milk or eating ice cream a literal pain
For some people, eating a dairy treat can lead to bloating, nausea and diarrhea
You might’ve experienced its effects yourself
If so, you may think of lactose intolerance as a defect rather than the norm
But did you know that most people in the world today are lactose intolerant – and that the condition itself was invented in the 1960s ? “Surely you mean discovered, not invented,” I hear you saying
As a historian who has traced the origins of nutrition-science ideas , I have chosen the word “invented” on purpose

Inventing lactose intolerance Variations in people’s ability to digest lactose first came to scientists’ attention after American dairy producers found a way to rid themselves of a postwar milk surplus
To offload what they couldn’t sell, they looked to the government to intervene
And it did, buying the excess and embedding it in school lunches and other places with publicly funded meals
Suddenly, many people who had not habitually drunk milk were consuming it regularly , including not only some Americans but also people overseas
Part of that same milk surplus found its way into school lunches in places such as Japan and Taiwan in the 1950s as the American government began to sell milk to allies during the Cold War
Longshou Elementary School students in Taiwan in 1964 eat an American aid lunch for the first time
National Archives of Taiwan , CC BY-NC-SA Many of the groups drinking milk regularly for the first time did not like it
Intrigued, scientists set up experiments to figure out why

In a 1966 study comparing how Black and white people incarcerated in Baltimore metabolized lactose, researchers found that Black participants had lower levels of lactase – the enzyme that breaks down lactose – in their guts

To the white scientists conducting this study, the trouble that the Black prisoners had digesting milk looked like an “ inborn error of metabolism .” They assumed that the normal human state was lactose tolerance and that the lactose intolerant had inherited a genetic mutation

It was only after years more work with research participants of many races that experts realized that, as one National Institutes of Health official put it in 1981, “lactose intolerance is a normal physiological condition , shared by every adult animal except for certain ethnic and racial groups in man.” People of northern European descent, it turned out, were the weird ones
It was their ancestors who had passed down a genetic mutation – one that made them able to digest milk after infancy
In short, what scientists discovered in the 1960s was that different bodies process milk differently
What they invented was the idea that lactose intolerance is a defect
Accepting that framing would mean nearly two-thirds of the human population – the estimated prevalence of lactose intolerance worldwide – is defective
Instead of acknowledging that dairy-free diets can be healthy, people innovated ways to overcome this supposed disability so everyone could consume more
Milk is advertised in China as essential to health, even though most of the population is lactose intolerant

Ng Han Guan/AP Photo Nutritional imperialism Lactose intolerance is one example of what I call nutritional imperialism : a way of thinking that treats white diets as the norm and everyone else’s as an aberration

Nutritional imperialism was common in the 20th century , when scientists thought that not only milk-rich but also meat-heavy diets were best; they considered diets outside of the United States and Europe too vegetarian
Some also argued that wheat flour, not rice, ought to be the universal staple
Besides faulty lactose digestion, nonwhite bodies were accused of other failures, too, such as aldehyde dehydrogenase deficiency , an inability to digest alcohol quickly
The less technical term for this may be more familiar: Asian flush
Such differences might have been thought of as variety, just another way of being human
Many people today have inherited and perpetuated this way of thinking without knowing it, including those who are deemed deficient by it

In 1959, the director of Japan’s nutrition bureau declared that “ rice-eating peoples ” such as the Japanese were “resigned and passive” and could correct this by imitating Western diets and switching to wheat
Milk is ubiquitous in grocery stores in China

Shwangtianyuan/Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA Today, the most prominent scientist promoting the idea that Asian flush is a disease is a geneticist of Taiwanese descent who started a research consortium to study “ the most common human enzymopathy in the world .” The Chinese Nutrition Society placed a tall glass of milk next to its 2022 Food Guide Plate – never mind estimates that the vast majority of Han Chinese, the largest ethnic group in China and worldwide , are lactose intolerant
Turning sickness back into difference Science that pathologizes difference helps racism persist
In recent years, white supremacists have embraced the concept of lactose intolerance as a distinguishing debility of nonwhite people

Social media users have copied and pasted a map of the geographic distribution of lactose tolerance originally published in the scientific journal Nature into racist chat threads on the online discussion forum 4chan
In 2017, internet trolls disrupted an anti-racist art installation with neo-Nazi chants and messily downed jugs of milk to accentuate their white identity
Turning a lactose-digestion difference into a deficiency has done more to reinforce narratives of racial hierarchy than to improve public health
So here’s a suggestion: If you enjoy eating dairy, keep doing it; if you don’t, don’t – and know that there is nothing wrong with you

<title>The United States’ human rights practices are taking a nosedive</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755769/original/file-20260824-50-oxf58z.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2024%2C1349&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Police detain a man during a June 2025 protest in Paramount, Calif., where federal immigration authorities had conducted operations.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Immigration%20Raids%20Los%20Angeles/36daa935dae64874b6b18cfa52394770/photo">AP Photo/Eric Thayer</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, how is the U.S. government performing in terms of human rights? Listening to politicians, it can be difficult to know. </p>

<p>On one hand, some have pointed to a <a href="https://www.ossoff.senate.gov/press-releases/new-sen-ossoff-investigation-uncovers-over-1000-credible-reports-of-human-rights-abuses-in-immigration-detention/">number of</a> <a href="https://www.padilla.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/padilla-advocates-for-protection-against-election-interference-amid-trump-election-chaos/">potential human</a> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/sep/26/james-comey-indictment-reaction">rights</a> <a href="https://menendez.house.gov/media/press-releases/menendez-crockett-and-ramirez-call-for-investigation-demand-faa-stop-helping-ice-hide-secret-ghost-flights">abuses</a> committed by the U.S. government inside and outside its borders in the past two years.</p>

<p>On the other hand, while marking the United States’ 250th anniversary this year, <a href="https://www.rev.com/transcripts/america-250-keynote-address">President Donald Trump</a> called the country “the home of freedom,” “the land of liberty” and “the most extraordinary, most exceptional, most incredible nation ever to exist on the face of the earth.”</p>

<p>“We’re doing better now than we’ve ever done before,” he said.</p>

<p>So which is it? </p>

<p>According to many of the <a href="https://humanrightsmeasurement.org/">human</a> <a href="https://www.politicalterrorscale.org/">rights</a> <a href="https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataverse/HumanRightsScores">data</a> <a href="https://cirights.com/">sources</a> available, the U.S. <a href="https://www.vox.com/2019/6/7/18656568/usa-human-rights-report-police-shooting-voter-suppression">lags behind</a> most other high-income democracies – countries that are both members of the <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/about/members-partners.html">Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development</a> and <a href="https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/opendata/world-bank-country-classifications-by-income-level-for-2024-2025">classified as high income</a> by the World Bank. The U.S.’s poor performance spans civil and political rights, such as the right <a href="https://rightstracker.org/metric/torture?income=hi&amp;cgroup=oecd">to be free from torture</a> and the right <a href="https://rightstracker.org/metric/participation?income=hi&amp;cgroup=oecd">to political participation</a>, as well as economic and social rights, including the rights to <a href="https://rightstracker.org/metric/health?income=hi&amp;cgroup=oecd">health</a> and <a href="https://rightstracker.org/metric/food?income=hi&amp;cgroup=oecd&amp;as=hi">food</a>.</p>

<p>In fact, the U.S. has been a relatively poor performer across many of these rights for <a href="https://theconversation.com/americans-are-not-as-well-off-as-people-in-peer-nations-us-safety-nets-shortfalls-show-up-in-global-data-284987">quite some time</a>, regardless of the political party in power. </p>

<p>Even accounting for the U.S.’s prior poor practices, however, new <a href="https://rightstracker.org/">data from the Human Rights Measurement Initiative</a> shows that in 2025 the country’s civil and political rights performance <a href="https://rightstracker.org/country/USA">deteriorated even further</a>. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=I_ZelvYAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">human rights scholar</a> who has been measuring human rights practices for 20 years – and as one of <a href="https://humanrightsmeasurement.org/the-team/">HRMI’s co-founders</a> – I believe this data raises serious questions about the United States’ commitment to human rights.</p>

<h2>How are rights practices measured?</h2>

<p>Governments rarely publish accurate information on their own human rights abuses, so the task of measuring them typically falls to advocates and scholars. </p>

<p>Historically, <a href="https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/RQ85GK">most</a> <a href="https://cirights.com/">international</a> <a href="https://www.politicalterrorscale.org/">measures</a> of <a href="https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights">civil and political rights</a> have depended on public reports from the <a href="https://www.state.gov/reports-bureau-of-democracy-human-rights-and-labor/country-reports-on-human-rights-practices/">U.S. State Department</a>, <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/annual-report-archive/">Amnesty International</a>, <a href="https://www.hrw.org/previous-world-reports">Human Rights Watch</a> or news organizations. </p>

<p>However, these reports cannot cover every human rights violation that experts know about, especially in countries with low government transparency or high levels of repression.</p>

<p>Thus, data produced using those sources will show fewer abuses than those that have actually occurred and will be more accurate about some places than others. Further, the Trump administration has changed one of the most important sources of human rights information, the U.S. State Department’s <a href="https://www.state.gov/reports-bureau-of-democracy-human-rights-and-labor/country-reports-on-human-rights-practices/">Country Reports on Human Rights Practices</a>, to contain more bias in favor of the administration’s foreign allies and <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/state-department-rolls-scaled-back-human-rights-report/story?id=124587579">less information on human rights abuse overall</a>.</p>

<p>Since 2017, <a href="https://humanrightsmeasurement.org/">HRMI</a> has used <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0022343320959688">a different approach</a>. Recognizing the problems with public reports, we collect information directly from researchers for human rights organizations, human rights lawyers and others, asking them about governments’ practices across several rights and using a statistical model to assess their information and ensure that the resulting metrics are comparable across countries. The result is a robust dataset that includes information previously missing from public reports. </p>

<p>Today, HRMI’s <a href="https://rightstracker.org/">civil and political rights dataset</a> covers 62 countries, with more added every year.</p>

<h2>How does the US compare?</h2>

<p>According to the <a href="https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/RQ85GK">Human Rights Scores dataset</a>, which uses publicly available information to score more than 190 countries on physical integrity rights – such as the rights to be free from torture, killing, forced disappearance and political imprisonment – the U.S. never ranked higher than 81st from 2001 to 2021 or higher than 109th from 2010 to 2021.</p>

<p>Indeed, from 2003 to 2021, the United States’ score was either the worst or the second-worst every year among <a href="https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/opendata/world-bank-country-classifications-by-income-level-for-2024-2025">high-income</a> <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/about/members-partners.html">OECD member states</a>, which include the United Kingdom, Japan and New Zealand. </p>

<p>The Human Rights Scores dataset has not been updated past 2021, but HRMI’s data collected since that time suggests that the pattern has continued. </p>

<p>Among the six high-income OECD countries on which HRMI currently collects data, the U.S. has been the <a href="https://rightstracker.org/metric/physint?income=hi&amp;cgroup=oecd">worst performer for physical integrity rights</a> since 2017.  </p>

<p>It has also frequently been rated as the <a href="https://rightstracker.org/metric/empowerment?income=hi&amp;cgroup=oecd">worst performer on “empowerment rights,”</a> or the rights to assembly, association, opinion, expression, political participation, religion and belief.</p>

<h2>What changed in 2025?</h2>

<p>Even starting from this poor position, the U.S.’s civil and political rights practices <a href="https://rightstracker.org/country/USA">dramatically worsened in 2025</a>. HRMI measures nine civil and political rights, and the U.S. significantly worsened on eight of them.</p>

<p>These were not small changes. Measured against every significant change HRMI has recorded since 2017, the U.S. showed the largest decline ever observed for the right to be free from <a href="https://rightstracker.org/country/USA?tab=report-physint">forced disappearance</a> and for the right to freedom of <a href="https://rightstracker.org/country/USA?tab=report-empowerment">religion and belief</a>. </p>

<p>The U.S. showed the second-largest decline ever observed for the right to be free from <a href="https://rightstracker.org/country/USA?tab=report-physint">arbitrary or political arrest</a> and for the right to <a href="https://rightstracker.org/country/USA?tab=report-empowerment">opinion and expression</a>.</p>

<p>The U.S. also showed major declines in the rights to be <a href="https://rightstracker.org/country/USA?tab=report-physint">free from torture</a> and <a href="https://rightstracker.org/country/USA?tab=report-physint">extrajudicial killing</a>, and the right to <a href="https://rightstracker.org/country/USA?tab=report-empowerment">political participation</a> – that is, the right to participate in one’s government via free and fair elections, to take part in public affairs and to have access to public service. U.S. scores likewise fell in the right to <a href="https://rightstracker.org/country/USA?tab=report-empowerment">assembly and association</a>, which are, respectively, the rights to peacefully gather in public or private and to form or join groups and organizations. </p>

<h2>What caused the scores to fall?</h2>

<p>Human rights experts <a href="https://rightstracker.org/country/USA?tab=atrisk">raised several issues</a> that led to these declines. For instance, the U.S.’s worsened scores for the rights to be free from arbitrary detention, disappearance and torture were tied to the <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/location/americas/north-america/united-states-of-america/report-united-states-of-america/">expanded use of practices</a> such as <a href="https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/ice-deports-3-u-s-citizen-children-held-incommunicado-prior-to-the-deportation">incommunicado</a> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/dec/04/alligator-alcatraz-human-right-violations-amnesty-report">detention</a> and <a href="https://www.acludc.org/press-releases/federal-court-requires-trump-comply-warrantless-arrests/#:%7E:text=In%20December%202025%2C%20the%20court,before%20a%20warrant%20can%20be">warrantless arrest</a> by ICE and other immigration-related agencies. </p>

<p>While <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/jan/04/ice-2025-deaths-timeline">several killings occurred during ICE operations</a> in 2025, the worsened extrajudicial killing score was also tied to the country’s use of airstrikes against boats in the Pacific and Caribbean, which caused the deaths of <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/location/americas/north-america/united-states-of-america/report-united-states-of-america/">at least 123 people</a> in 2025 alone.</p>

<p>Other changes enacted in 2025 contributed to large declines in the U.S.’s rights scores, including <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/sep/20/immigrant-rights-groups-trump-crackdown">crackdowns on anti-ICE demonstrations</a> and government <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/oct/01/academic-freedom-us">pressure on universities</a>, including limits on <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/location/americas/north-america/united-states-of-america/report-united-states-of-america/">free speech</a> and <a href="https://www.universityworldnews.com/post.php?story=20260116140044901">class subjects</a>.</p>

<p>Last year also saw <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2025/09/19/trump-threatening-broadcast-station-licenses-explained.html">threats to television networks</a> over political expression, <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/state-voting-laws-roundup-october-2025">restrictions on mail-in voting</a>, state measures <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/10/us-civil-rights-group-documents-broad-attack-on-muslim-life-in-2025">targeting American Islamic organizations</a> by labeling them <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/11/21/cair-sues-texas-governor-over-unconstitutional-terror-designation">“foreign terrorist organizations”</a> and an executive order focused on <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/feb/07/trumps-executive-order-anti-christian-bias">eradicating “anti-Christian bias</a>.”</p>

<p>While current HRMI data does not yet cover 2026, early indicators are not promising, with continued <a href="https://www.hrw.org/report/2026/06/25/dying-in-detention/rising-deaths-in-an-expanding-us-immigration-detention-system">abuses by ICE</a>, further <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/05/usa-death-toll-in-campaign-of-extrajudicial-killings-at-sea-nears-200/">killings in international waters</a> and allegations of <a href="https://statesunited.org/resources/politicized-prosecutions-rule-of-law/">attempts to use government powers</a> to <a href="https://statesunited.org/resources/us-v-splc/">punish</a> <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/18/nx-s1-5936406/abc-and-disney-sue-fcc-alleging-first-amendment-violations">critics</a>.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/286538/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

He is also an associate professor of international affairs and the director of the Center for the Study of Global Issues (GLOBIS) at the University of Georgia. He has previously received funding from the National Science Foundation, the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, the Ford Foundation, Amnesty International, the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the International Development Research Centre, and the Human Rights Measurement Initiative Charitable Trust. </span></em></p></content>

On one hand, some have pointed to a number of potential human rights abuses committed by the U.S. government inside and outside its borders in the past two years

On the other hand, while marking the United States’ 250th anniversary this year, President Donald Trump called the country “the home of freedom,” “the land of liberty” and “the most extraordinary, most exceptional, most incredible nation ever to exist on the face of the earth.” “We’re doing better now than we’ve ever done before,” he said

So which is it? According to many of the human rights data sources available, the U.S. lags behind most other high-income democracies – countries that are both members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and classified as high income by the World Bank

The U.S.’s poor performance spans civil and political rights, such as the right to be free from torture and the right to political participation , as well as economic and social rights, including the rights to health and food
In fact, the U.S. has been a relatively poor performer across many of these rights for quite some time , regardless of the political party in power

Even accounting for the U.S.’s prior poor practices, however, new data from the Human Rights Measurement Initiative shows that in 2025 the country’s civil and political rights performance deteriorated even further

As a human rights scholar who has been measuring human rights practices for 20 years – and as one of HRMI’s co-founders – I believe this data raises serious questions about the United States’ commitment to human rights
Protesters walk through a shopping center after attending a demonstration for Renee Good, who was fatally shot by an ICE officer in Minneapolis in January 2026

AP Photo/Charlie Riedel How are rights practices measured? Governments rarely publish accurate information on their own human rights abuses, so the task of measuring them typically falls to advocates and scholars
Historically, most international measures of civil and political rights have depended on public reports from the U.S
State Department , Amnesty International , Human Rights Watch or news organizations
However, these reports cannot cover every human rights violation that experts know about, especially in countries with low government transparency or high levels of repression
Thus, data produced using those sources will show fewer abuses than those that have actually occurred and will be more accurate about some places than others
Further, the Trump administration has changed one of the most important sources of human rights information, the U.S
State Department’s Country Reports on Human Rights Practices , to contain more bias in favor of the administration’s foreign allies and less information on human rights abuse overall
Since 2017, HRMI has used a different approach

Recognizing the problems with public reports, we collect information directly from researchers for human rights organizations, human rights lawyers and others, asking them about governments’ practices across several rights and using a statistical model to assess their information and ensure that the resulting metrics are comparable across countries
The result is a robust dataset that includes information previously missing from public reports
Today, HRMI’s civil and political rights dataset covers 62 countries, with more added every year

How does the US compare? According to the Human Rights Scores dataset , which uses publicly available information to score more than 190 countries on physical integrity rights – such as the rights to be free from torture, killing, forced disappearance and political imprisonment – the U.S. never ranked higher than 81st from 2001 to 2021 or higher than 109th from 2010 to 2021
Indeed, from 2003 to 2021, the United States’ score was either the worst or the second-worst every year among high-income OECD member states , which include the United Kingdom, Japan and New Zealand
The Human Rights Scores dataset has not been updated past 2021, but HRMI’s data collected since that time suggests that the pattern has continued
Among the six high-income OECD countries on which HRMI currently collects data, the U.S. has been the worst performer for physical integrity rights since 2017
It has also frequently been rated as the worst performer on “empowerment rights,” or the rights to assembly, association, opinion, expression, political participation, religion and belief
Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Illinois on Oct. 11, 2025
AP Photo/Adam Gray What changed in 2025? Even starting from this poor position, the U.S.’s civil and political rights practices dramatically worsened in 2025
HRMI measures nine civil and political rights, and the U.S. significantly worsened on eight of them

Measured against every significant change HRMI has recorded since 2017, the U.S. showed the largest decline ever observed for the right to be free from forced disappearance and for the right to freedom of religion and belief
The U.S. showed the second-largest decline ever observed for the right to be free from arbitrary or political arrest and for the right to opinion and expression

The U.S. also showed major declines in the rights to be free from torture and extrajudicial killing , and the right to political participation – that is, the right to participate in one’s government via free and fair elections, to take part in public affairs and to have access to public service
U.S. scores likewise fell in the right to assembly and association , which are, respectively, the rights to peacefully gather in public or private and to form or join groups and organizations
What caused the scores to fall? Human rights experts raised several issues that led to these declines

For instance, the U.S.’s worsened scores for the rights to be free from arbitrary detention, disappearance and torture were tied to the expanded use of practices such as incommunicado detention and warrantless arrest by ICE and other immigration-related agencies

While several killings occurred during ICE operations in 2025, the worsened extrajudicial killing score was also tied to the country’s use of airstrikes against boats in the Pacific and Caribbean, which caused the deaths of at least 123 people in 2025 alone

Other changes enacted in 2025 contributed to large declines in the U.S.’s rights scores, including crackdowns on anti-ICE demonstrations and government pressure on universities , including limits on free speech and class subjects

Last year also saw threats to television networks over political expression, restrictions on mail-in voting , state measures targeting American Islamic organizations by labeling them “foreign terrorist organizations” and an executive order focused on eradicating “anti-Christian bias .” While current HRMI data does not yet cover 2026, early indicators are not promising, with continued abuses by ICE , further killings in international waters and allegations of attempts to use government powers to punish critics
Chad Clay is the co-founder and Methodology Research and Design Lead of the Human Rights Measurement Initiative
He is also an associate professor of international affairs and the director of the Center for the Study of Global Issues (GLOBIS) at the University of Georgia

title: The long afterlife of QAnon conspiracy theories haunting American politics

<title>The long afterlife of QAnon conspiracy theories haunting American politics</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755785/original/file-20260824-50-8gja2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C4%2C3536%2C2357&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A woman touches a QAnon patch on her outfit during a Christian prayer gathering in Washington on May 17, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/MajorglobalnewsmomentsofMayinAPphotos/ef74d423c38d41f0964d45eab16b5cf1/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=QAnon&amp;currentItemNo=87&amp;startingItemNo=50&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>On Election Day in 2024, as voters cast their ballots, Elon Musk <a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/1853612871877329188?s=20">posted a campaign music video</a> supporting Donald Trump’s bid for president. </p>

<p>Set to Van Halen’s “Jump,” with a montage of 1980s cultural references and images of Trump in various strongman poses, the video includes a line about “PATRIOTS” in which the “O” turns into a “Q,” a reference to the online conspiracy theory QAnon. </p>

<p>Started on the online forum website 4chan in 2017, <a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/QAnon">QAnon spread false, far-right theories on social media</a> about a shadowy cabal of satanic pedophiles among the political elite, which Trump was purportedly fighting alongside a mysterious ally named “Q.”</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://commarts.wisc.edu/staff/hannah-matthew/">scholar of conspiracy theories and extremism</a>, I’ve watched QAnon seep from the margins into mainstream American politics over the past decade. While Q stopped posting in 2022, <a href="https://www.npr.org/2024/12/30/nx-s1-5230801/qanon-capitol-riot-social-media">the movement did not disappear</a>. As we near the 10-year anniversary of QAnon, these theories continue to haunt America’s politics.</p>

<h2>The afterlife of QAnon</h2>

<p>Building on the 2016 “<a href="https://www.politico.com/story/2016/12/pizzeria-accused-child-sex-slaves-232220">Pizzagate</a>” conspiracy theory, which claimed Democrats were trafficking children in the basement of a pizza restaurant based on interpretations of Hillary Clinton’s leaked emails, <a href="https://www.adl.org/resources/backgrounder/qanon">QAnon appeared on 4chan in October 2017</a> with claims that Clinton was about to be arrested. </p>

<p>That’s when someone calling himself Q claimed to be an intelligence operator trying to expose the “deep state,” a purported shadow government secretly controlling global events in pursuit of a satanic agenda. QAnon invited users to <a href="https://doi.org/10.11645/17.1.3277">build the theory</a> by decoding messages on social media. That work, Q claimed, would expose a satanic cabal of pedophiles among the elites. </p>

<p>The theory is an example of what author Naomi Klein has called a “<a href="https://theintercept.com/2020/12/08/great-reset-conspiracy/">conspiracy smoothie</a>,” mixing existing theories into a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/20563051211036064">vast conspiracy map</a>, which absorbs existing conspiracy theories about events such as 9/11 or the JFK assassination into itself. The result is a sprawling theory combining paranoid interpretations of current events with historical conspiracies. </p>

<p>Polls suggest that <a href="https://prri.org/press-release/new-prri-report-reveals-nearly-one-in-five-americans-and-one-in-four-republicans-still-believe-in-qanon-conspiracy-theories/">20% of Americans</a> had favorable views of QAnon as late as 2022.  </p>

<p>Many of Trump’s nominations for high-ranking posts were figures who had previously been considered on the fringes of national politics. Some of them have brought conspiracy theories into the highest echelons of government.</p>

<p>FBI Director Kash Patel, for example, has been <a href="https://www.npr.org/2024/12/09/nx-s1-5213692/kash-patel-conspiracy-theories-fbi">sympathetic to QAnon</a>. He appeared on <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/investigations/2024/12/07/kash-patel-trump-fbi-pick-appeared-on-qanon-themed-internet-show/76829357007/">a show hosted by a QAnon influencer</a> before being selected to run the agency. And Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has advocated <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/saradorn/2024/11/15/rfk-jrs-conspiracy-theories-heres-what-trumps-pick-for-health-secretary-has-promoted/">anti-vaccination conspiracy theories</a> also shared by QAnon.</p>

<h2>QAnon haunts Washington</h2>

<p>I’m particularly fascinated by the ghost of QAnon – how the theory continues to haunt politics today. Philosophers call this tendency “<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/books/booksblog/2011/jun/17/hauntology-critical">hauntology</a>”: Political ideas and movements may die, but they continue to haunt our present.</p>

<p>Q’s ideas have not dissipated. It’s what I call QAnon’s afterlife, or the transformation of QAnon from a conspiracy theory to a political vocabulary. In fact, the movement’s vocabulary quickly began to appear in official government circles at the start of Trump’s second term.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755787/original/file-20260824-50-b1wplz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A letter Q is seen next to a social media account visible on a smartphone." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755787/original/file-20260824-50-b1wplz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755787/original/file-20260824-50-b1wplz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755787/original/file-20260824-50-b1wplz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755787/original/file-20260824-50-b1wplz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755787/original/file-20260824-50-b1wplz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755787/original/file-20260824-50-b1wplz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755787/original/file-20260824-50-b1wplz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">In this photo illustration, Donald Trump’s Truth Social account is seen on a mobile device with an image of a QAnon sticker on his lapel in September 2022.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-this-photo-illustration-donald-trumps-truth-social-news-photo/1243276677?adppopup=true">Olivier Douliery/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In March 2026, for example, the official X account for the White House posted a photo of a mustachioed fighter pilot with the QAnon tagline “<a href="https://x.com/WhiteHouse/status/2030674844707070226?s=20">Patriots are in Control</a>.” While the phrase may pass as mundane, I believe it is a clear reference to QAnon language, <a href="https://archive.4plebs.org/pol/thread/147075091/#147106598">first used by Q in October 2017</a>. </p>

<p>The U.S. Department of Labor <a href="https://x.com/USDOL/status/2007933111729021305?s=20">posted the same phrase over an image of Trump</a> in January 2026. Lori Chavez-DeRemer, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/apr/25/lori-chavez-deremer-resign-trump-labor-secretary-staff">who has publicly advocated deep state conspiracies</a>, ran the department until she resigned on April 20, 2026. </p>

<p>And Musk, the former head of the <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/department-of-government-efficiency-171139">Department of Government Efficiency</a>, celebrated America’s 250th birthday with an AI-generated video called “<a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2073723522653069812?s=20">Sweet Land</a>.” This post generated buzz because it referenced QAnon and prompted an online <a href="https://x.com/emmamcqeown/status/2073863417941885290?s=20">scavenger hunt for Q symbols</a>.</p>

<h2>QAnon goes to war</h2>

<p>Amid the U.S. war with Iran, some government officials have turned to QAnon for inspiration. </p>

<p>The official account for the Pentagon’s chief technology officer, Emil Michael, has posted propaganda using Q catchphrases as military slogans. For example, the department posted <a href="https://x.com/DoWCTO/status/2076987001614516623?s=20">a picture of a Marine saluting Trump</a> with the phrase “Trust the Plan.”  </p>

<p>On Truth Social, Trump posted a meme of himself on the deck of a battleship with the words “<a href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/116586041697060377">It was the Calm Before the Storm</a>,” a cryptic phrase <a href="https://youtu.be/BREos5woyXc?si=wquI2qkruoHuX0C4">first used by Trump</a> while meeting with military leaders in October 2017. Almost exactly one month later, <a href="https://archive.4plebs.org/pol/thread/147547939/#147586045">the phrase appeared as a central QAnon concept</a>. </p>

<p>The use of Q phrases by government agencies during wartime has <a href="https://x.com/truestormyjoe/status/2063065784809627677?s=20">excited online conspiracy theorists</a>. They see it as an official endorsement that “the storm” will soon be upon us, a time of upheaval and punishment of the shadowy deep state. For these conspiracy theorists, Trump and Q will bring about “<a href="https://x.com/Saulito46107740/status/2084606427939688844?s=20">the storm</a>,” to be followed by <a href="https://x.com/shadygrooove/status/2084474996186034399?s=20">a golden age</a>. </p>

<h2>The QAnon style of American politics</h2>

<p>Whether or not these references to Q posts by official government accounts are truly ideological or simply trolling is less relevant than the effect they have. </p>

<p>Official uses of Q language have invigorated conspiracy theorists to <a href="https://x.com/TheRubberDuck79/status/1861277135672901833?s=20">advance new theories</a>, undermining <a href="https://x.com/redpilldispensr/status/1975494744714182723?s=20">public health</a>, <a href="https://x.com/holonabove/status/2077948633861828960?s=20">governance</a> and <a href="https://x.com/TheQeye_/status/2074549941796536760?s=20">civil society</a>.</p>

<p>And <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/epstein-files-179022">the Jeffrey Epstein files</a>, which have <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/investigation-reveals-doj-withheld-epstein-files-mentioning-trump">exposed the late financier’s</a> private network and financial dealings, have only lent credence to <a href="https://x.com/KAGdrogo/status/2018413996492353635?s=20">QAnon theories among believers</a>. That’s because <a href="https://8kun.top/qresearch/res/884810.html#885005">Q referenced Epstein Island</a> in drops of information on 8chan and other message boards.</p>

<p>I believe these ghostly eruptions of QAnon conspiracy theories into the public will only continue to divide Americans at a time of social and economic crisis.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289784/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: ‘Male’ and ‘female’ plugs and connectors – gendered language for the ends of garden hoses, electrical cords and pipe fittings sparks debate
url:
<title>‘Male’ and ‘female’ plugs and connectors – gendered language for the ends of garden hoses, electrical cords and pipe fittings sparks debate</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755826/original/file-20260824-60-pbqogl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=418%2C819%2C6781%2C4521&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Male and female or plug and socket?</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/green-electric-power-plug-and-cable-on-white-royalty-free-image/145573737">artpartner-images/The Image Bank via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Hopefully to mean “I hope”; singular “they”; “primary bedroom” instead of “master bedroom” – all are examples of recent language changes.</p>

<p>How do such changes develop? And what happens when people push back against them?</p>

<p>We studied a pair of ubiquitous terms currently undergoing change: “male” and “female” used to describe connector ends. Consider this sentence from Jinko Solar’s <a href="https://jinkosolar.us/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/PV-JK03M-Connector-Installation-Manual-LH.pdf">directions for installing connectors</a> on its photovoltaic products: </p>

<blockquote>
<p>“Insert the male connector into the female connector once the nut is fully tightened. Connection of male and female connectors is complete when an audible click is heard.”</p>
</blockquote>

<p>“Male” and “female” show up across industries, such as when plumbers talk about pipe fittings, when firefighters talk about hose connections, when electricians talk about twist lock plugs, when welders talk about quick disconnects, when IT specialists talk about RS-232 ports, and when audio professionals talk about TRS cables.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<p>The use of male and female for connectors isn’t only technical jargon for specialists; it reaches into laypeople’s everyday lives. Ace Hardware, for example, advertises an “<a href="https://www.acehardware.com/departments/lawn-and-garden/watering-and-irrigation/garden-hose-connectors/74895">ABS Threaded Male/Female Hose Mender Clamp</a>” to anyone looking to repair a broken garden hose. </p>

<h2>What’s the problem with male and female?</h2>

<p>Professionals in some industries, including <a href="https://a-us.storyblok.com/f/570395326227278/x/e98b8cd20f/inclusivelanguageguide.pdf">audiovisual</a>, <a href="https://www.citt.org/cgi/page.cgi/citt_news.html/What_s_New/Terminology_Work_Group">theater</a> and <a href="https://www.acm.org/diversity-inclusion/words-matter">IT</a>, have argued that these terms are, at best, <a href="https://medium.com/@L10nLab/it-starts-with-words-unconscious-bias-in-gender-race-and-class-in-tech-terminology-7473d4e84da5">inappropriate as direct analogs to sexual intercourse</a> and, at worst, exclusionary in their assumption of binary gender. </p>

<p>Further, when people use male and female, they tend to refer to the two types of connector ends as genders. The <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_of_connectors_and_fasteners">Wikipedia entry on male and female</a> connectors is one example. But as <a href="https://collegepublishing.sagepub.com/products/designing-and-conducting-gender-sex-and-health-research-1-234666">research over the past few decades</a> has made clear, <a href="https://theconversation.com/genetic-testing-cannot-reveal-the-gender-of-your-baby-two-genetic-counselors-explain-the-complexities-of-sex-and-gender-217631">gender and sex are not synonymous</a>.</p>

<h2>What do editors and style guides say?</h2>

<p>As two researchers specializing in linguistic approaches to the <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/jo-mackiewicz-6012177">study of technical communication</a>, <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=HPg4FSkAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=sra">particularly technical editing</a>, we wondered what editors thought about male and female for connector ends. Had they heard of arguments against their use? Had they advised writers to avoid the terms?</p>

<p>Using a Qualtrics survey distributed to groups like <a href="https://aceseditors.org/">ACES</a>: The Society for Editing, we asked editors what they <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/TPC.2026.3712307">would do with this sentence</a>: “Insert the two-pronged male end into the female receptacle in the console.” These editors worked on a variety of genres, such as instructions, API documentation and technical manuals under a range of job titles, including technical writer, technical editor and copy editor. Twenty-seven editors responded to our question, and we interviewed three of the respondents afterward.</p>

<p>Editors’ responses split pretty evenly among the three options that we provided: Maintain the terms as they are, query the author about their use, or edit the words – that is, replace them with different words. Ten editors responded that they would keep the words, nine said they’d ask the author about their use of the words, and eight said that they would replace the terms with something else.  </p>

<p><iframe id="DMNyw" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/DMNyw/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Bar chart showing three responses pretty evenly split between editors who would leave gendered language the same, edit it, or ask the writer about it."></iframe></p>

<p>This mix of approaches tracks with style guides’ varied treatment of “male” and “female.” The latest version of the <a href="https://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org/home.html">Chicago Manual of Style</a> does not mention male/female in the context of connectors. Neither does the <a href="https://apstylebook.com/">Associated Press Stylebook</a> or the American Psychological Association’s <a href="https://www.apa.org/about/apa/equity-diversity-inclusion/language-guidelines">Inclusive Language Guide</a>. More surprisingly, neither does the IT-focused <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/style-guide/welcome/">Microsoft Writing Style Guide</a>.</p>

<p>Two major style guides for the tech industry do now include entries about male/female language, both prohibiting the usage. The <a href="https://developers.google.com/style">Google Developer Documentation Style Guide</a> calls for alternatives like “plug” and “socket.” The <a href="https://support.apple.com/guide/applestyleguide/welcome/web">Apple Style Guide</a> recommends plug and socket or “port.” In addition, certain professional organizations have begun to use alternatives, such as <a href="https://www.acm.org/diversity-inclusion/words-matter">plug</a> or “<a href="https://tsdca.org/app/uploads/USITT-TSDCA-Sound-Documentation-Recommendations_April_2022_APPROVED.pdf">pin</a>” and <a href="https://soundgirls.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/PAMARecommendationsforNeutralNomenclatureinProAudio.pdf">socket</a>.</p>

<h2>What does the opposition say?</h2>

<p>People against this change make three arguments.</p>

<p>The first says that changes for inclusivity signify a “<a href="https://ell.stackexchange.com/users/11747/donewiththis">woke-gone-mad</a>” culture that coddles <a href="https://www.reddit.com/r/computers/comments/8ebx1i/comment/dxu4mzk/">overly sensitive people</a>. Such arguments have accompanied most, if not all, changes aimed at making language more inclusive. Arguments about singular “they” stretched on for decades, finally resulting in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10572252.2023.2236671">widespread style-guide adoption</a>.</p>

<p>Once-acceptable gendered terms, such as <a href="https://www.babbel.com/en/magazine/are-gendered-words-like-mankind-inherently-sexist">mankind</a> and <a href="https://grammarphobia.com/blog/2018/10/ess-words.html">stewardess</a>, have been replaced with alternatives. So have other terms considered insensitive, such as <a href="https://inclusivenaming.org/word-lists/tier-1/_master-slave/">master/slave</a> and <a href="https://inclusivenaming.org/word-lists/tier-1/blackhat-whitehat/">blackhat/whitehat</a>. In each case, the lexical transition met pushback.</p>

<p>The second argument says “male” and “female” are the clearest terms because they capitalize on the iconic relationship between human and other animal genitalia and connector ends. <a href="https://www.quora.com/How-are-cables-named-as-female-or-male/answer/Bill-Jones-385">From this perspective</a>, the bug is the feature.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>However, this supposedly inherent relationship doesn’t necessarily hold. Take the example of a photovoltaic solar-panel connector where the so-called female side is more of a protrusion than the so-called male. The male connector is designated that way because it contains the pin. Such complications have led to conventionalized uses of male and female that aren’t necessarily obvious.</p>

<p>The third argument is perhaps the most important: The widespread use of the terms across industries <a href="https://qr.ae/py4Fj1">makes the terms the ones people expect</a>. Thus, the terms facilitate communication. This argument contends that switching terminology would constitute a colossal challenge. Such comments also indicate an inertia problem of language change: Many people won’t use alternative terms like plug and socket until others in their professional community do.</p>

<h2>The slow evolution of language</h2>

<p>Anti-diversity, equity and inclusion executive orders from the White House that <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/03/07/us/trump-federal-agencies-websites-words-dei.html">aim to ban words</a> like “inclusion” might stem the already slow movement toward nongendered terms like plug and socket.</p>

<p>But if history is any precedent, English speakers of the future will think the use of male and female for connector ends as odd as people today consider long-ago typical usages of “<a href="https://www.dictionary.com/articles/nice-guys">nice” to mean “ignorant”</a> and <a href="https://www.englishgrammar.org/garbage-went-animal-entrails-everyday-trash/">“garbage” to mean “guts.”</a></p>

<p>That is, they’ll think it’s queer.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/270142/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Shifting the cleanup cost of packaging waste to companies could encourage greener packaging – but only if states are aligned</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/752081/original/file-20260804-50-rtr1m3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C80%2C1920%2C1280&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Some state legislatures are seeking ways to alleviate anxieties about plastic waste. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Shampoo_Aisle_Shoppers_Drug_Mart_Edmonton_Early_2020.jpg">Rowanswiki/Wikimedia Commons</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Standing in your local retail store, it can be mind-boggling to try to weigh the pros and cons of all the packaging options. Take shampoo, for example. Shampoo can come in a rigid plastic bottle, a flexible squeeze tube, a refillable metal canister or a solid bar in a paperboard box. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/iPf529urxw8?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A viral video of the “packaging guy” from comedian Jimmy Rees highlights just how arbitrary packaging design decisions seem.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Trying to make environmentally friendly or socially conscious purchasing decisions can be a challenge, as product packaging can feature various sustainability claims. You might see a product listed as any of the following: recyclable, compostable, refillable, made with recycled content or bio-based materials, carbon or plastic neutral, cruelty free, fair trade, promoting responsible forest management, or a myriad of other labels. </p>

<p>Disposing of the empty packaging poses a similar challenge. Which materials are recyclable, compostable or trash is generally determined at the local municipal level, based on what packaging items regional recycling and compost markets will accept.</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=jMWQem4AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">As an environmental policy researcher</a>, however, I’ve seen the potential in a <a href="https://theconversation.com/packaging-generates-a-lot-of-waste-now-maine-and-oregon-want-manufacturers-to-foot-the-bill-for-getting-rid-of-it-165517">policy approach gaining traction</a> for packaging in the United States: extended producer responsibility, or EPR. This approach could radically change what packaging companies choose to use and what happens to that packaging after you throw it out.</p>

<h2>What is extended producer responsibility?</h2>

<p>Extended producer responsibility policies are based on the <a href="https://www.lse.ac.uk/granthaminstitute/explainers/what-is-the-polluter-pays-principle/">“polluter pays” principle</a>, which reasons that the parties responsible for generating pollution should bear the cost of managing it. As the name implies, EPR extends responsibility to producers. </p>

<p>Determining exactly who counts as the producer and what type of responsibility is extended, however, depends on the particular law. Generally speaking, these policies aim to hold big companies such as General Mills or PepsiCo liable for what happens to the cereal boxes, chip bags and soda cans their products are packaged in. </p>

<p>By requiring these brand owners to fund – and in some cases operate – recycling systems, EPR shifts the burden of waste management off local taxpayers. As producers incorporate these costs, the assumption is that they will redesign their packaging in ways that <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/extended-producer-responsibility_9789264256385-en.html">reduce their overall environmental impact</a>. </p>

<p>First implemented in Europe in the early 1990s, this policy approach has gained considerable global traction. <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/extended-producer-responsibility_9789264256385-en.html">Over 400 mandatory EPR laws</a> covering various products, including packaging, cars, electronics, batteries, textiles and more, have been adopted in various countries. </p>

<p>Producers generally pay fees to a producer responsibility organization, based on the amount and type of packaging material they sell. This organization then uses the money to pay for the collection and processing of packaging materials for recycling.</p>

<p>These programs have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wasman.2022.05.019">improved recycling rates</a>. But they have been less successful at <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10640-022-00696-9">encouraging packaging design improvements</a>. </p>

<p>As EPR policies evolve, policymakers are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wasman.2023.05.033">experimenting with new approaches</a> that encourage producers to make sustainable packaging design changes. For example, one new policy mechanism – eco-modulation – adjusts producers’ fees up and down based on certain design considerations. With eco-modulation, producers that incorporate recycled material into their packaging may pay less in fees. On the other hand, producers that use difficult-to-remove labels that make their packaging hard to recycle may face higher fees.</p>

<p><iframe id="8a5SQ" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/8a5SQ/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A chloropleth map depicting which states participate in EPR laws, with MN, CO, WA, MD, CA, OR, ME and HI highlighted."></iframe></p>

<h2>Packaging policies gaining ground in the US</h2>

<p>Unlike the EPR policies in Europe that are enacted at the national level and guided by <a href="https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/40/oj/eng">European Union-wide regulation</a>, EPR in the United States is emerging at the state level.</p>

<p>Since 2021, <a href="https://www.americanbar.org/groups/environment_energy_resources/resources/trends/2026-july-aug/producers-pay-for-packaging/">seven U.S. states</a> have passed extended producer responsibility laws to hold companies accountable for the boxes, bottles, jugs, jars and cans their products come in. Over a dozen additional states are <a href="https://epr.sustainablepackaging.org/policies">considering EPR policies</a> but haven’t yet passed laws. </p>

<p>The fragmented landscape of packaging regulations across the U.S. has <a href="http://doi.org/10.1016/j.wasman.2026.115465">sparked calls to standardize policies</a> to make it easier for companies to comply and increase overall effectiveness.</p>

<h2>Understanding the patchwork of policies</h2>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/752083/original/file-20260804-50-c4lhk3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A store aisle containing several bins filled with food items, with scoops to scoop them out." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/752083/original/file-20260804-50-c4lhk3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/752083/original/file-20260804-50-c4lhk3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/752083/original/file-20260804-50-c4lhk3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/752083/original/file-20260804-50-c4lhk3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/752083/original/file-20260804-50-c4lhk3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/752083/original/file-20260804-50-c4lhk3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/752083/original/file-20260804-50-c4lhk3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">Depending on policy design, packaging laws could incentivize the adoption of more reusable packaging or refillable packaging options, such as this bulk aisle in Magog, Quebec.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Erin Victor</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>I <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wasman.2026.115465">recently conducted a survey</a> of waste policy experts, including researchers, government officials, producer responsibility organizations, consultants and civil society actors. These experts spoke directly to why these policies are so fragmented. The experts said that EPR policies should shift packaging waste management costs to producers. But they had differing views on the overall goals of the policies, how to measure program success and how to structure fees.</p>

<p>For example, some experts saw EPR as a tool for funding improvements to local recycling systems. Others stressed that simply shifting the recycling costs to producers is not enough. They argued that these policies must also reduce the producers’ environmental impacts.</p>

<p>The survey participants also prioritized different packaging design changes. For example, some participants said EPR policies should focus on litter reduction, such as encouraging producers to use nondetachable bottle caps. Others wanted to see more focus on reusable packaging or the adoption of bio-based or compostable packaging. </p>

<p>Without clear agreement on what makes packaging truly sustainable, regulations often rely on goals, such as requiring 100% of packaging be recyclable or compostable. However, these material attributes <a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.9b07910">do not always reduce environmental impacts</a>.</p>

<h2>Why do policy inconsistencies matter?</h2>

<p>As states adopt policies with conflicting goals and design standards, the emerging patchwork of laws creates an impossible blueprint for companies looking to redesign their packaging. For example, switching to a compostable bottle may be <a href="https://policypickup.substack.com/p/finding-where-compostable-packaging">rewarded in one state and penalized in another</a>. </p>

<p>Even without a national EPR policy, more consistent goals, targets and design incentives across states could help policymakers better unlock the full potential of these laws. Under the current policies, large multinational companies are likely to treat compliance fees as just a cost of doing business. Coordinating the rules would send a clearer signal to producers to design greener packaging.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/284283/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
